agents.name: Lomustine
agents.explanation: Lomustine is an oral nitrosourea chemotherapy that can reach the brain. It damages DNA and interferes with cell division. Its effects on healthy blood-forming cells can appear several weeks after the dose and can build up over successive cycles. This explains the long gap between doses and the need for continuing blood tests.
agents.watch: This is one dose on Day 1, not a daily medicine. If an extra dose is taken, get urgent advice even if you feel well. Keep blood tests after the dose and report fever, bruising, bleeding, new cough or breathlessness.
risks: Delayed and cumulative low blood counts
Rare second cancers and fertility effects

agents.name: Bevacizumab
agents.type: Targeted antibody given into a vein
agents.mechanism: Blocks the blood-vessel growth signal VEGF
agents.explanation: Bevacizumab binds VEGF, a signal involved in making and maintaining blood vessels. Blocking this signal can change the blood supply and leakiness of tumour vessels. It can also affect normal vessels, which helps explain high blood pressure, protein in the urine, bleeding, clots and slower wound healing. A scan change does not by itself prove that the tumour has stopped growing.
agents.watch: Report bleeding, severe abdominal pain, new chest or breathing symptoms, sudden neurological changes, headaches with visual changes, and any operation or wound problem. Keep blood-pressure and urine checks.
risks: High blood pressure and rare PRES neurological syndrome
Protein in the urine and kidney injury
Blood clots, stroke or heart attack
Slow wound healing and wound complications
Infusion reactions and rare severe allergy
Fertility effects and harm to a pregnancy

passport_visit_note: Record the cycle number, exact treatment day, medicines actually received or held, safety tests and symptom changes. Record bevacizumab visits separately within each lomustine cycle.
anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects are anchored to the retained detailed body illustration. Brain symptoms may reflect the tumour, treatment or another medicine; effects may involve more than one area. This is not the complete side-effect list.
anatomy: Keep BP checks. Severe headache, visual change, seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty needs urgent assessment.
Report unusual bruising or bleeding. Heavy bleeding, sudden chest pain or collapse needs emergency help. Counts can fall weeks after lomustine.
New breathlessness, cough or chest pain needs prompt advice. Severe breathing difficulty needs emergency help.
New chest pain, a painful swollen leg or sudden one-sided weakness needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain or collapse needs emergency help.
Protein in urine may cause no early symptoms. Keep urine and kidney checks; report swelling, reduced urine or a major change.
Severe or persistent abdominal pain, vomiting or blood in stool needs urgent advice. Follow the prescribed nausea and bowel plan.
Tell the team about operations, dental procedures and wounds. Report wounds that open, fail to heal or show infection.
Discuss fertility and contraception before treatment. Do not breastfeed during therapy; obtain written medicine-specific advice.

day_groups.title: Two medicines, different routes
day_groups.body: Lomustine is a single oral dose; bevacizumab is an infusion. Keep the anti-sickness plan for lomustine.
day_groups.action: Confirm cycle number and the exact capsule supply before taking it.

day_groups.body: Return for bevacizumab on Day 22. No extra lomustine is scheduled. Continue blood-pressure, urine and blood checks.

chronology_notes.title: A treatment record is not a prescription
chronology_notes.text: The team may delay, alter or stop a component after reviewing symptoms, blood tests, organ function and previous toxicity. Do not restart a held medicine or add a replacement dose yourself.

chronology_notes.title: Lomustine is one dose, not daily
chronology_notes.text: Only the authorised Day 1 dose belongs to this cycle. Do not take a further course before six weeks and a new team decision. Taking repeated daily doses can cause serious harm. If a dose is missed or vomited, contact the team or pharmacist before taking any more. If an extra dose is taken, seek urgent clinical advice straight away even if you feel well; do not wait for symptoms.

chronology_notes.title: Delayed marrow effects
chronology_notes.text: Current lomustine product information advises blood counts weekly for at least six weeks after a dose. Low counts may be delayed and cumulative, so keep checks even when you feel well or the next treatment is postponed.

chronology_notes.title: Infusion visits and procedures
chronology_notes.text: Bevacizumab needs review around surgery and wound healing. Tell the team before an operation, dental procedure or other intervention, and do not assume an infusion is safe because a calendar interval has passed.

administration_text: Take lomustine only once on the authorised Day 1. The pharmacist must confirm the total dose, capsule strengths, how to take it and anti-sickness timing. Do not open or crush capsules or take another dose to replace a missed or vomited one without advice. Bevacizumab is given into a vein. The usual first infusion lasts 90 minutes; later infusions may take 60 and then 30 minutes if tolerated. Checks and observation add time. Report flushing, rash, breathing difficulty, dizziness or other new symptoms immediately.

support.title: Lomustine nausea prevention
support.text: Lomustine has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed prevention and rescue plan around the single dose. Contact the team if nausea or vomiting prevents fluids or essential medicines; do not automatically repeat a vomited chemotherapy dose.

support.title: Bevacizumab support is separate
support.text: Bevacizumab alone has minimal emetic potential. Routine anti-sickness drugs or steroid premedication are not automatically required for every infusion; the team may prescribe specific medicines after a previous reaction or for another reason.

support.title: Blood pressure, urine and wound care
support.text: Keep prescribed blood-pressure medicine and urine checks. Follow the team’s plan for any home measurements. Report wounds and upcoming surgery or dental treatment early, so timing and healing can be assessed before another infusion.

support.title: Separate steroid, seizure and bowel plans
support.text: Keep prescribed steroids and seizure medicines on their own schedules. Ask about missed or vomited doses. Agree a bowel plan if other medicines cause constipation and check interactions before adding a medicine.

monitoring_summary: Before starting: Blood count, kidney/liver tests, glucose, urine protein, blood pressure and cardiac history/examination; NCCP lung testing for patients at high risk. Current lomustine SmPC additionally advises baseline lung-function assessment. During treatment: Regular blood count, kidney/liver tests and urine protein; blood pressure before each bevacizumab dose and after treatment. Current lomustine SmPC advises weekly blood counts for at least six weeks after a dose and continuing lung assessment. MRI and neurological review follow your individual treatment plan. Echocardiography is considered only when indicated, including previous anthracycline treatment or chest-wall radiotherapy. If taking warfarin, INR is checked weekly until stable and before subsequent cycles.

sections.title: Taking the treatment
sections.text: Take lomustine only once on the authorised Day 1. The pharmacist must confirm the total dose, capsule strengths, how to take it and anti-sickness timing. Do not open or crush capsules or take another dose to replace a missed or vomited one without advice. Bevacizumab is given into a vein. The usual first infusion lasts 90 minutes; later infusions may take 60 and then 30 minutes if tolerated. Checks and observation add time. Report flushing, rash, breathing difficulty, dizziness or other new symptoms immediately.

sections.title: Missed, vomited or held medicine
sections.text: If a capsule dose is missed or vomited, call the oncology team or pharmacist before taking more. Do not double up or use leftover capsules. An infusion or capsule held for toxicity needs a new team decision.

sections.title: Medicine and supplement review
sections.text: Bring all prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines, vitamins and supplements to review. Include steroids, seizure medicines, anticoagulants and any recent antibiotics or antifungals. Tell the team before starting or stopping a medicine.

sections.title: Surgery, procedures and wounds
sections.text: Tell all treating teams that you receive bevacizumab. Major surgery needs an appropriate treatment interval and a fully healed wound before restarting; minor and dental procedures also need individual advice. Do not decide timing yourself or rely on the wallet stamp.

sections.title: Capsule supply and handling
sections.text: Lomustine is supplied as an unlicensed medicine in this NCCP protocol. Confirm pharmacy supply in advance. Keep the labelled pack away from children and do not open or crush capsules. Return unused chemotherapy to the pharmacy; contact staff if swallowing or handling is difficult.

sections.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
sections.text: Discuss fertility preservation and contraception before starting. Treatment can harm a pregnancy. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Ask for the written medicine-specific precautions and the required periods after stopping; these may differ between products.

sections.title: Appointments and transport
sections.text: Before starting: Blood count, kidney/liver tests, glucose, urine protein, blood pressure and cardiac history/examination; NCCP lung testing for patients at high risk. Current lomustine SmPC additionally advises baseline lung-function assessment. During treatment: Regular blood count, kidney/liver tests and urine protein; blood pressure before each bevacizumab dose and after treatment. Current lomustine SmPC advises weekly blood counts for at least six weeks after a dose and continuing lung assessment. MRI and neurological review follow your individual treatment plan. Echocardiography is considered only when indicated, including previous anthracycline treatment or chest-wall radiotherapy. If taking warfarin, INR is checked weekly until stable and before subsequent cycles.

sections.title: Help with the daily plan
sections.text: Agree help with prescriptions, travel, calls and symptom notes if fatigue, memory, sight or weakness makes these difficult. Your preferences guide who is involved. Keep the printed plan and real urgent contacts together.

sections.title: Off-label treatment and infusion decisions
sections.text: Bevacizumab for glioblastoma is outside its licensed indication in Ireland. The team should explain the reason for using it, expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives as part of consent. Any rapid infusion outside the standard schedule has a separate local consent and governance process.

evidence.title: EORTC 26101: evidence and schedule limits
evidence.intro: The randomised trial compared lomustine plus bevacizumab with lomustine alone after glioblastoma progression.
evidence.population: Patients with first progression of glioblastoma after chemoradiotherapy.
evidence.interpretation: Adding bevacizumab delayed measured progression in the trial but did not improve overall survival. Treatment goals and burdens need an individual discussion.
limitations: The trial used bevacizumab 10 mg/kg every two weeks, not this NCCP 7.5 mg/kg every three weeks schedule. No trial survival or response number is assigned to this dose schedule.
Trial lomustine dose escalation and treatment duration do not replace the current NCCP regimen.
Historical pathology, patient selection and later treatments limit individual prediction.

chapters.title: Understanding your particular glioma
chapters.intro: Your diagnosis includes the tumour’s cells, molecular findings and behaviour, not just the word brain cancer.

items.title: The name and location
items.text: A glioma is a tumour arising in the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different types. Cancer that travels to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and follows a different pathway.

items.title: Grade is not the same as stage
items.text: Glioma reports combine the tumour type, grade and molecular findings. Grade is not a measure of spread around the body: a grade 4 brain tumour does not mean body-wide metastases. Ask your specialist to explain older terms in your records.

items.title: IDH and 1p/19q
items.text: Changes in the IDH genes and loss of chromosome regions 1p and 19q help classify certain gliomas. The pattern of results matters. These are usually tumour-sample tests; they do not by themselves show that a change runs in the family.

items.title: MGMT promoter methylation
items.text: The MGMT gene makes a protein that repairs a particular type of DNA damage. Methylation in its control region can reduce that repair and inform discussion of temozolomide benefit. This is a tumour-tissue result, not a blood marker or a personal survival percentage.

items.title: A useful diagnosis record
items.text: Keep the exact pathology diagnosis, sample date, grade and available molecular results together. Label a result as pending or not tested when appropriate. Ask whether further pathology review would affect the plan.

chapters.title: Tests and scans: what each one tells you
chapters.intro: Safety blood tests, tumour tissue tests and MRI answer different questions.

items.title: Safety blood tests
items.text: A full blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests assess other aspects of treatment safety. Follow the blood-test schedule even when you feel well or the scan is reassuring.

items.title: MRI and neurological review
items.text: MRI gives detailed pictures of the brain. The team also checks symptoms, movement, speech, thinking and daily function. Before scanning, tell staff about implants, metal, kidney problems or previous contrast reactions, and ask for help if the scan worries you.

items.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
items.text: Treatment-related changes can resemble tumour growth on MRI; this is called pseudoprogression. The specialist interprets the scan with symptoms and may need another scan or further assessment. Report worsening symptoms promptly rather than assuming a scan change is harmless.

items.title: An individual follow-up timetable
items.text: Record the next MRI and the contact who will explain it. Your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous results determine the interval. Other scans or blood markers are ordered for a specific reason, not automatically before every cycle.

items.title: Keep results with decisions
items.text: Mark tests as booked, done and reviewed so the next action is clear. Contact the named service about a missing result. Do not change chemotherapy or steroids in response to a report without instructions.

chapters.title: Brain symptoms, medicines and when to call
chapters.intro: Symptoms may reflect the tumour, swelling, treatment, another medicine or a separate illness.

items.title: Know your usual symptoms
items.text: Before treatment, note your usual walking, strength, speech, sight, memory, sleep and seizure pattern. Record new changes and their timing. A trusted person can help if you want them involved.

items.title: Urgent neurological changes
items.text: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.

items.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
items.text: Steroids may reduce swelling around a brain tumour. If needed, ask for a written dose, review date and reduction plan; do not stop suddenly or adjust the dose yourself. Report infection symptoms, marked thirst, weakness or troublesome sleep or mood changes.

items.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
items.text: Take prescribed seizure medicine on its own schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and how to manage a breakthrough seizure. Do not switch or stop it yourself. Anyone giving a rescue medicine needs the personal instructions and training.

items.title: Safety at home and outside
items.text: Discuss driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery with your team, taking account of symptoms and seizures. Individual medical and licensing advice is needed. Occupational therapy can help make daily routines safer.

chapters.title: Your overall treatment plan and choices
chapters.intro: Treatment should account for the tumour and the life you want to lead.

items.title: Understand the sequence
items.text: Place biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and follow-up on one plan. Concurrent means treatments overlap; adjuvant means treatment follows the main treatment. A new phase can require different doses, tests and support medicines.

items.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
items.text: Ask what treatment can reasonably achieve for your tumour and which effects matter most to you. Discuss benefits, burdens, alternatives and the reasons for a pause or stop.

items.title: Put evidence in context
items.text: A study result applies to a particular group, diagnosis and schedule. Older studies may use different tumour names. Ask which evidence fits your plan; an average cannot forecast your response or lifespan.

items.title: Discuss options available to you
items.text: Ask about suitable trials, another specialist opinion and other treatment or symptom-care options. Your multidisciplinary team explains what is appropriate and available for you.

items.title: Make room for your priorities
items.text: Bring up thinking, independence, family time, work and the side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for time, written notes or a supporter if that helps you weigh the choices.

chapters.title: Living well, rehabilitation and support
chapters.intro: Practical and symptom support can begin alongside anticancer treatment.

items.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
items.text: Tell the team about changes in memory, language, attention, sight or planning. Rehabilitation can involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or psychology. Ask for practical help with routines and medicines.

items.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
items.text: Use your prescribed nausea and bowel plan and report problems early. Ask for dietitian help if intake or weight falls. Adapt movement to your balance and strength, and ask the team to assess fatigue that disrupts daily life.

items.title: Emotional support and carers
items.text: Tell the team about changes in mood, behaviour or coping. Patients and carers may each need psychological or practical support. Agree who can receive information and ask for help before caring becomes overwhelming.

items.title: Work, transport and finances
items.text: Tell the nurse or social worker about travel, employment, finances and caring responsibilities. Arrange practical help with medicines or appointments if symptoms make those tasks difficult.

items.title: Supportive care and future wishes
items.text: Supportive and palliative care can help manage symptoms while treatment continues. When you are ready, discuss future care preferences and whom you want involved. Ask your team to help document these wishes.

items.title: Information that works on paper
items.text: Keep the latest paper schedule, medicine list, results plan and emergency contacts together. The treatment card helps others identify your regimen. It supports, but does not replace, the prescription and emergency instructions.

questions.a: Ask for written medicine plans and a named contact. Rehabilitation, practical support and a trusted helper may support the daily plan.

questions.q: Which symptoms mean I should call now?
questions.a: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Call urgently for bleeding, severe abdominal pain, chest symptoms, new headache with visual changes or wound problems. Tell the team about planned surgery before treatment.

questions.q: When do we review whether treatment is helping?
questions.a: Agree the next clinical and imaging review, what would count as benefit, how side effects will be weighed and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping.
